cards.title: J. S. Liptay
cards.prompt: One IBM engineer wrote the 1968 paper that argued the Model 85's fast buffer into existence off a simulation study. Name him, and give the one compatibility rule he said forced the cache to be filled and emptied with no help from the program.
cards.body: He was not inventing a cache, he was justifying one. Nineteen trace tapes, replayed cycle-by-cycle against an imaginary Model 85 whose whole memory ran at cache speed, came out at 81 percent of that ideal. His constraint, page 15: it must happen "without program assistance, since the Model 85 must be compatible with the rest of the SYSTEM/360 line."
cards.answer: J. S. Liptay. Because the Model 85 had to stay compatible with the rest of the System/360 line, the cache had to load and discard itself without program assistance — no program could address it or be allowed to detect it.

cards.title: $158,000 a month, none installed
cards.sub: March 1968 · Monthly Computer Census, Computers and Automation
cards.prompt: The 360/85 reached the trade-press census before it reached a customer. What monthly rental was listed against it, how many installations were counted, and which quarter were first customer shipments scheduled for?
cards.body: The census lists the 360/85 at $158,000 average monthly rental — against $138,000 for the 360/67 and $81,400 for the 360/75 — with a dash under date of first installation and 0 installed. The same issue's newsletter: "First customer shipments will be scheduled for the third quarter of 1969."
cards.answer: $158,000 a month, zero installed, first customer shipments scheduled for the third quarter of 1969.

cards.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache
cards.sub: IBM Systems Journal, Vol. 7, No. 1, 1968, pp. 15-21
cards.prompt: Name the primary document that specifies the Model 85 cache — journal, volume, number, year and pages — and give the footnote in it that says where the word "cache" came from.
cards.body: Seven pages. It carries the store-through rule, the validity bit, the channel path, the sector-and-block layout and the 0.968 hit probability. Its first footnote, and the whole provenance of the word: "The term cache is synonymous with high-speed buffer, as used in other Model 85 documentation."
cards.answer: J. S. Liptay, "Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache", IBM Systems Journal, Vol. 7, No. 1, 1968, pp. 15-21. Footnote 1: the term cache is synonymous with high-speed buffer, as used in other Model 85 documentation.

cards.title: Why an eviction is not data loss
cards.sub: 1968 → the cache in front of your database
cards.prompt: Transparency on the Model 85 forced two properties that every cache you use still has. Name both, and say which of them is the reason losing a cache entry is not losing data.
cards.body: Stores always update the store of record; and because nothing lives only in the cache, a sector can be dropped without moving a byte — change the address register, reset the validity bits, load a block. The second is why eviction is free, and why write-back caching is a different, riskier animal.
cards.answer: Writes go through to main storage (nothing lands only in the cache), and every cached byte is also in main storage. The second means an entry can vanish at any moment with no write-back and no data loss.
